title: What I Learned From Each of Them
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from Meditations by Marcus Aurelius, in the Jeremy Collier translation.
body: Of my grandfather Verus I have learned to be gentle and meek, and to refrain from all anger and passion. From the fame and memory of him that begot me I have learned both shamefastness and manlike behaviour. Of my mother I have learned to be religious, and bountiful; and to forbear, not only to do, but to intend any evil; to content myself with a spare diet, and to fly all such excess as is incidental to great wealth. Of my great-grandfather, both to frequent public schools and auditories, and to get me good and able teachers at home; and that I ought not to think much, if upon such occasions, I were at excessive charges.

Of him that brought me up, not to be fondly addicted to either of the two great factions of the coursers in the circus, called Prasini, and Veneti: nor in the amphitheatre partially to favour any of the gladiators, or fencers, as either the Parmularii, or the Secutores. Moreover, to endure labour; nor to need many things; when I have anything to do, to do it myself rather than by others; not to meddle with many businesses; and not easily to admit of any slander.

Of Diognetus, not to busy myself about vain things, and not easily to believe those things, which are commonly spoken, by such as take upon them to work wonders, and by sorcerers, or prestidigitators, and impostors; concerning the power of charms, and their driving out of demons, or evil spirits; and the like. Not to keep quails for the game; nor to be mad after such things. Not to be offended with other men’s liberty of speech, and to apply myself unto philosophy.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what did the author learn from his grandfather Verus?
options: To be gentle and meek, and to refrain from anger
To be ambitious and competitive
To distrust strangers
To value wealth above all else

questions.prompt: Per the passage, what kind of diet did the author's mother teach him to be content with?
options: A spare diet
A rich and varied diet
A diet of only fruit
Whatever diet was most expensive

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what two chariot-racing factions does the author mention?
options: The Prasini and the Veneti
The Parmularii and the Secutores
The Stoics and the Epicureans
The Romans and the Greeks

questions.prompt: Per the passage, what did his tutor teach him about doing tasks?
options: To do things himself rather than by others
To always delegate to servants
To finish tasks as quickly as possible
To ask his mother for help

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what did Diognetus teach him not to believe in?
options: Sorcerers and charm-workers who claim to drive out demons
The teachings of the Stoic philosophers
The value of public schools
The honesty of his own family

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the author credit his great-grandfather for his education?
options: His great-grandfather arranged good schools and private teachers for him, regardless of cost
His great-grandfather personally tutored him every day
His great-grandfather forbade him from attending public schools
His great-grandfather paid for his gladiator training

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what does the author's account of his mother suggest about her character?
options: She valued restraint, generosity, and avoiding wrongdoing even in intention
She was ambitious for wealth and status
She cared little for religion
She encouraged excess and luxury

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why did his tutor discourage him from favoring gladiators or racing factions?
options: To keep him from being consumed by partisan enthusiasm for spectacles
Because such spectacles were against the law
Because he had no interest in sports of any kind
Because the emperor had banned him from attending

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the overall point of the passage?
options: The author lists specific virtues and habits he owes to different people in his upbringing
The author complains about the failings of his family
The author argues that philosophy is a waste of time
The author describes the layout of the imperial palace

questions.prompt: As used in the passage, what does it mean that the author learned "shamefastness" from his father's memory?
options: Modesty
Boldness
Wealth
Ambition

questions.prompt: Per the passage, what did the author's mother teach him about intending evil?
options: To forbear not only doing but even intending evil
To confess any evil thought at once
That intentions do not matter, only actions
To punish evil intentions in others severely

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what two types of gladiators does the author mention?
options: The Parmularii and the Secutores
The Prasini and the Veneti
The Stoics and the Cynics
The Praetorians and the Legionaries

questions.prompt: Per the passage, what did his tutor teach him about admitting slander?
options: Not to easily admit of any slander
To repeat slander only if it were true
To report slander to the authorities
To ignore slander entirely without judgment

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what game involving quails did Diognetus discourage?
options: Keeping quails for fighting
Hunting quails for food
Racing quails against each other
Trading quails for money

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why did the author mention being taught to endure labor and need little?
options: To show the self-reliant, undemanding character his upbringing instilled in him
To explain why he became a soldier
To justify his later poverty
To criticize his tutor's harshness

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes the structure of the passage?
options: It attributes a specific virtue or lesson to each person who shaped the author's upbringing
It argues that all his teachers failed him equally
It focuses entirely on his mother's influence
It describes a single event from his childhood in detail

questions.prompt: As used in the passage, what does it mean to be "bountiful," as the author says he learned from his mother?
options: Generous
Cautious
Quiet
Strict
